records.name: Eswatini
records.summary_text: Eswatini is dangerous for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility.

records.name: Lesotho
records.summary_text: Lesotho demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (sodomy common-law crime struck down in 2012); the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by state and non-state actors (2024 UPR submission); no LGR; small organised community inside South Africa's geographic envelope.

records.name: Cabo Verde
records.summary_text: Cabo Verde is workable — Africa's most tolerant jurisdiction alongside South Africa's legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; Praia and Mindelo host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. No explicit GI protections and no LGR statute (administrative practice unclear), but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

records.name: Maldives
records.summary_text:
Maldives is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the Penal Code and sharia framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming Maldivians face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 HRC shadow report documents ICCPR violations). BUT: the tourist resort islands operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted on a resort; the risk concentrates in Malé and local islands.
